A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same IFeF-PINN research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original PDE-solving experiments, baseline comparisons, ablations, and spectral analysis in Section 6 and Appendix G.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds end-to-end training and hyperparameter ablations, an MFF comparison, and computational-cost measurements.

M1.justification: The latent Fourier-feature architecture, objectives, alternating training, and quadratic solve for linear PDEs are retained. Nonlinear optimization using gradient descent or L-BFGS already appears in v1 Section 3.2. v2 Section 3.4 and Algorithm 2 document that branch more explicitly, including update cadence and initialization options, without establishing a replacement of the underlying method.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate low- and high-frequency Helmholtz and convection problems, multiscale convection-diffusion, viscous Burgers, and the ten-frequency convection spectrum test. The added comparisons reuse this coverage. Correcting table labels to 4π and 60π matches the convection-diffusion parameters already specified in v1 Appendix F.1.

E2.justification: v2 adds Multi-scale Fourier Features (MFF; Wang et al., 2021b) as an evaluated comparator for both convection frequencies and convection-diffusion in Appendix G.1, Table 8. Table 3 also adds an end-to-end training control. The original Vanilla PINN, NTK, PINNsformer, and PIG comparisons remain.

E3.justification: Reported convection boundary-point counts change from 404/204 to 303/153 for the low-frequency case and from 404 to 303 for the high-frequency case (v1 Table 5; v2 Table 7). Low-frequency Helmholtz regularization changes from 1e-7 to 1e-6 (v1 Table 3; v2 Table 5). New experiments introduce joint-training controls, D/σ sweeps, and timing/memory metrics. These reported changes do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained RFF-removal and spectrum analyses, Section 6.4 adds a direct test of alternating versus end-to-end optimization on Helmholtz and Burgers problems, plus D and σ sensitivity studies on both Helmholtz frequencies. Appendix G.2 adds resource comparisons and separates upper- and lower-level computational costs. These substantially expand analysis of the method's components and practical behavior.

E5.justification: Both versions specify five independent random-seed runs, report boxplots with medians/IQRs/means and tables with means/standard deviations, and average the spectrum analysis over five runs. The additions use existing reporting conventions; no increased run count, new confidence-interval procedure, or significance testing is introduced.

E6.justification: The original Table 2 scores and retained result images are unchanged, but substantial results are added. Table 3 reports low-frequency Helmholtz error of 0.0088 for end-to-end training versus 0.0003 for IFeF; Table 8 reports MFF error of 0.350 for β=200 convection. Tables 4, 9, and 10 add sensitivity and resource measurements. These are additional comparisons and settings, not demonstrated improvements over earlier runs.

T1.justification: Appendices C.1–C.2 correct sign inconsistencies: the optimality condition becomes Qθ+c=0, the solution becomes -Q^-1c, and the corresponding hypergradient terms are corrected. Section 4.1 qualifies nonlinear solution-map regularity using a second-order sufficient condition and a local neighborhood. The principal convergence and approximation results and their proof structures remain.

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions, and main conclusion retain the same claims: latent Fourier features mitigate spectral bias, alternating training has convergence guarantees under assumptions, the architecture supports universal approximation, and experiments outperform existing baselines. The added evidence does not redefine these central contributions.

C2.justification: v2 explains warm starts as avoiding a zero-solution failure for homogeneous PDEs, interprets D/σ sensitivity and the end-to-end ablation, and attributes computational costs to particular components. It removes the detailed resampling warning from Remark 2 and the conclusion, although Table 1 and Appendix B.1 retain related limitations. These refine mechanisms and practical boundaries without replacing the main interpretation.

D1.justification: Section 6 replaces the future code-release promise with a repository address and a statement of availability. Section 3.4 supplies nonlinear update-frequency and initialization details, while Appendix G.2 provides measured training times and memory usage and identifies PIG's default L-BFGS optimizer. Most architecture, hardware, and optimizer documentation is retained.

R1.justification: v2 develops an explicit empirical comparison with the already-cited input-space Fourier-feature approach and removes v1's suggestion that low-dimensional inputs limit its asymptotic approximation capability. The Zienkiewicz et al. reference is removed. PIG and PINNsformer publication updates and other bibliographic corrections represent the same cited works.

P1.justification: The overall narrative and section order remain recognizable. Local revisions give nonlinear PDEs a dedicated subsection, replace a remark, shorten theorem presentations, add ablation and appendix subsections, and introduce acknowledgments. Most existing prose and appendix proofs are retained rather than extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 3, 4, and 8–10 and separate nonlinear-training pseudocode. Figures 3–4 remove their exact-solution panels while retaining the prediction/error displays. The manuscript is also comprehensively reformatted into the ICLR template, changing typography, text width, spacing, and placement of displays.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens validation through the missing end-to-end control, D/σ sensitivity studies, an input-space MFF comparison, and computational-cost measurements. Corrected appendix signs and a concrete code address also improve usability. However, reporting inconsistencies limit confidence in some additions: Table 8 gives a low-frequency IFeF mean/SD of 7.0e-5/1.6e-3, incompatible with the stated five-run interpretation for nonnegative errors, while Appendix E still says σ=1 throughout despite Table 4's sweep. The net improvement is supported but qualified.
